qs.q:
UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
The municipal authority ______ of turning the old industrial port into a smart pedestrian zone.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 3: 'think of/about' mang nghĩa 'đang suy tính/cân nhắc' là hành động chủ ý nên chia ở thì Hiện tại tiếp diễn: is thinking.

qs.q: With vertical farms and solar-glass windows, the new high-rise tower looks ______ against the blue sky.
qs.ex: Sau linking verb 'looks' dùng tính từ: modern.

qs.q: Smart street sensors can monitor air quality and traffic flow, making the city more ______ for residents.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: liveable = đáng sống.

qs.q: Why ______ you ______ the soup like that? Is there something wrong with the herbs from our roof garden?
qs.ex: Động từ 'smell' chỉ hành động chủ ý 'ngửi thử' chia ở thì tiếp diễn: are / smelling.

qs.q: The herb tea grown on our balcony garden smells ______, so everyone in the family loves it.
qs.ex: 'smells' là linking verb chỉ tính chất tỏa hương của trà → đi với tính từ: wonderful.

qs.q: Many city ______ worry that ubiquitous security cameras in smart cities may reduce their personal privacy.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: city dwellers = cư dân thành thị.

qs.q: I ______ the chief architect at 2 p.m. tomorrow to discuss the new cycle path network.
qs.ex: Động từ 'see' mang nghĩa 'gặp gỡ/hẹn gặp ai' dùng ở thì Hiện tại tiếp diễn cho kế hoạch tương lai: am seeing.

qs.q: As electric buses replace diesel vehicles, the air in the urban centre is becoming ______.
qs.ex: Sau linking verb 'is becoming' dùng tính từ: cleaner.

qs.q: Replacing car lanes with wide ______ zones encourages people to walk and interact with neighbours.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: pedestrian zones = các khu phố đi bộ.

qs.q: My sister ______ that smart home appliances will give families more free time in the future.
qs.ex: 'think that...' diễn tả quan điểm/niềm tin (stative verb) → không chia tiếp diễn, dùng 'thinks'.

qs.q: Roof gardens on ______ buildings help absorb rainwater and cool down concrete apartments in summer.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: high-rise buildings = các tòa nhà cao tầng.

qs.q: The mayor’s plan for underground waste-collection pipes sounds ______ to all environmental engineers.
qs.ex: Sau linking verb 'sounds' dùng tính từ: practical.

qs.q: Driverless electric shuttles will operate smoothly along dedicated lanes to prevent rush-hour ______.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 3: prevent rush-hour traffic jams = ngăn chặn tắc đường giờ cao điểm.

qs.q: Look! The technician ______ the solar battery on the smart lamppost right now.
qs.ex: Dấu hiệu 'Look!... right now' → Hiện tại tiếp diễn: is checking.

qs.q: Shared neighbourhood parks and community centres help strengthen the ______ of community among apartment residents.
qs.ex: Cụm từ Unit 3: sense of community = ý thức gắn kết cộng đồng.

**DESIGNING OUR FUTURE SMART CITY**
Right now, our school and community **(1)**______ a special campaign focused on smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living, and we invite everyone to join us. Many city dwellers and planners regularly participate in smart technologies in future urban centres, where **(2)**______ a positive difference every week. Taking part in these activities helps young people learn how to use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams. Educators and families also note that **(3)**______ expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment. This month, our organisers **(4)**______ practical workshops on how to build sustainable and liveable smart cities, so please **(5)**______ the activities in your neighbourhood. Your active **(6)**______ will help build a better future for everyone!
(Adapted from Global Success – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living in Unit 3: Cities of the Future.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new smart technologies in future urban centres.
b. In the past, many people did not pay enough attention to smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living.
c. Today, however, both city dwellers and planners realise how important it is to build sustainable and liveable smart cities.

**PERSPECTIVES ON CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
In recent years, smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of city dwellers and planners recognise the importance of smart technologies, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**connected**</u> these practices into their daily routines in future urban centres. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to build sustainable and liveable smart cities.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how smart technologies can expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should build sustainable and liveable smart cities, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role in future urban centres. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living matters for the long-term future. Young people who see city dwellers and planners model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, smart technologies not only use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams today but also expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**MAKING CITIES OF THE FUTURE PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to build sustainable and liveable smart cities may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed smart technologies help city dwellers and planners use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams. At the same time, these practices expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment and foster stronger cooperation in future urban centres.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in smart technologies has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**liveable**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. City dwellers and planners can start with simple steps in future urban centres, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**dweller**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of city dwellers and planners valued smart technologies, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres, teenagers were twice as likely to use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When city dwellers and planners work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
When people first decide to focus on smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced smart technologies are far more effective when built step by step, helping city dwellers and planners use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how smart technologies can use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising smart technologies independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 3: Cities of the Future to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? When city dwellers and planners see their close friends willingly engage in smart technologies, they are far more likely to join in and use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
Why do many high school students agree that smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living is important, yet still find it difficult to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, city dwellers and planners can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on smart technologies. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 3: Cities of the Future report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, smart technologies stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
Why do many high school students agree that smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living is important, yet still find it difficult to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, city dwellers and planners can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on smart technologies. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 3: Cities of the Future report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, smart technologies stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**COMBINING TRADITIONAL VALUES WITH MODERN TOOLS IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
In the digital age, some commentators worry that modern technology might distract young people from smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living. Yet recent educational projects show that when used wisely, digital tools can actually strengthen smart technologies. Shared mobile calendars, reminder apps and online group checklists make it easier than ever for city dwellers and planners to use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams.
Of course, technology alone cannot solve every problem. Researchers warn against relying passively on apps while ignoring face-to-face communication, as <u>**they**</u> are only tools in the hands of users. <u>**Digital tools should serve as a practical bridge to support daily cooperation rather than a replacement for genuine human interaction.**</u>
When families and classmates combine smart reminders with warm personal encouragement, they can <u>**preserve**</u> the core spirit of Unit 3: Cities of the Future. For example, a quick evening message can remind everyone to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres before gathering for a friendly conversation.
Ultimately, blending modern convenience with timeless values helps communities <u>**enhance**</u> their daily routines and expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment in a sustainable way.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living. Rather than treating Unit 3: Cities of the Future as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on smart technologies. Through these authentic tasks, city dwellers and planners discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 3: CITIES OF THE FUTURE**
Practising smart technologies is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps city dwellers and planners expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)

Educators studying smart cities, green skyscrapers and sustainable urban living have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to use AI sensors to save energy and eliminate traffic jams.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to build sustainable and liveable smart cities in future urban centres this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps city dwellers and planners expand rooftop gardens and pedestrian zones for a greener environment with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 3: Cities of the Future)
